product.title: Vietnamese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Vietnamese: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Vietnamese builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Vietnamese grammar is surprisingly light for an English speaker: verbs never change, nouns have no plural, there is no gender and no articles, and time is marked by three small words for already / in progress / will. This course takes advantage of that from Unit 1 and puts its real effort into the one thing that is genuinely hard: the six tones — plus the unfamiliar vowels and the letters that don't sound the way English readers expect.

blocks.text: There is one fact about Vietnamese that beginners are almost never told, and it deserves to be on the first page of every textbook: **Vietnamese grammar is one of the simplest you will ever meet** — in many places simpler than English itself.

Not a little simpler. Simpler down to the bone. Verbs **never change** — not for the person, not for the tense, not for anything. Nouns **have no plural**: one form for one and for many. There is no **grammatical gender**, no *der/die/das*. There are **no articles** — no "a", no "the". Adjectives come **after** the noun ("house beautiful", not "beautiful house") — one of the few things you will have to flip. And question words **stay where the answer would go**: *Anh đi đâu?* is literally "you go where?", not "where are you going?".

Most surprising of all: Vietnamese marks time with **three separate little words** — *đã* = already (past), *đang* = in the middle of (-ing), *sẽ* = will. No verb forms to memorize: just a word placed in front, and you can even drop it when the time is clear from context — "Yesterday I go there" is perfectly good Vietnamese.

Even the thing that usually throws beginners — **classifiers** such as *cái*, *con*, *quyển* — is not entirely new. English already says "a **loaf** of bread", "two **head** of cattle", "a **piece** of paper"; Vietnamese simply does it with every noun you count. And the pronoun system that shifts with age (*anh*, *chị*, *em*, *cô*, *chú*) is not an alien world either: think of calling someone "sir", "ma'am", "auntie" or "big brother" — only here it is how you say "you" and "I".

So where is the difficulty? In **one place only**, and it lies outside grammar: **sound**. Vietnamese has six tones, and a tone here is not decoration — it distinguishes words. *Ma* means ghost, *mà* means but, *má* means mother, *mả* means grave, *mã* means horse, *mạ* means rice seedling. Six different words, one spelling; only the rise and fall of the voice tells them apart. English has nothing like it. Add a few vowels that English mouths don't make — *ơ*, *ư*, *â*, *ă* — and letters that sound different from what you'd guess, like *d* pronounced *z* and *x* pronounced *s*.

That is why this course is deliberately lopsided. Grammar is explained quickly, because much of it simply isn't there. Sound gets the long treatment: it comes first, before Unit 1, and it comes back again and again — every word in the whole course comes with a **Say it** column, from the first word to the last.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: This course asks one thing only: **say it out loud**. A tonal language cannot be learned with your eyes — if you read *phở* silently, your head fills it in with a flat English tone, and that mistake hardens into a habit within days.
Do one unit per sitting, 20–30 minutes. At five days a week, all twenty units are done in under two months.
Don't skip the pronunciation chapter on the next pages. It is not an extra; it is the only truly hard part of the whole course, and everything after it rests on it.

This course uses **northern Vietnamese (Hà Nội)** — the variety of national broadcasting, understood throughout the country. Important differences from the southern variety (Sài Gòn) are pointed out where they come up.

blocks.text: Happy learning. *Chúc bạn học tốt!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: Twenty units, each built to clear away one of the spots that really trip learners up — without long explanations of things Vietnamese simply doesn't have.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, 20 to 30 minutes, and asks nothing of you except a willingness to read out loud.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read only the Vietnamese, without glancing below, and **out loud**. Only then read the translation.
**Literal translation** — the small line under each sentence. It shows Vietnamese word order word by word. Watch for the spots where it sounds **odd** in English — that is where the lesson is.
**Notes** — things that are visible in the dialogue but that you may not have noticed.
**Grammar boxes** — the rule you just saw at work, explained after you have seen it, not before.
**Extra sections** — reference tables, ready-made phrases, cultural notes.
**Vocabulary** — every new word in the unit, with its pronunciation.
**Exercises** and **answer key** — four sets of questions; do them all before you open the key.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: After finishing a new unit, quickly go back over the unit from **two days ago** and the one from **a week ago** — just read the dialogue out loud, two minutes per unit.
This is not a time-saving tip; it is the only way Unit 3 will still be alive in your head when you reach Unit 15.

blocks.text: One last rule, and for Vietnamese it is stricter than for any other language: **say it out loud, and exaggerate the tones**. English speakers almost always say tones too flat, because English uses pitch for whole sentences, not for single words. Better to sound like you are singing than to sound flat — flat is not understood at all; exaggerated is understood with a smile.

This is the most important part of the whole course, and it comes first because you will use it on every page that follows. Read it twice. Better to spend a full hour here than to redo the whole course with the wrong sounds.

The good news first: Vietnamese is written in the **Latin alphabet** — called *quốc ngữ* — and its spelling is **faithful to its sounds**. A letter sounds the same wherever it stands. No silent letters, no surprises like *though*/*tough*. Once you know the value of each letter, you can read any word you've never seen — including names of people and streets.
The less good news: **the letters do not have their English values**, and above the letters sit the tones. This chapter sorts out both.
Six tones — the heart of the whole course

Every Vietnamese syllable has a tone, and the tone is **part of the word**, not a matter of style. Changing the tone means changing the word — exactly like changing a letter. If you say *má* (mother) with the tone of *mã*, you don't sound odd; you say "horse".

head: Tone
Mark
Example
Meaning
What it sounds like
rows: level in the middle, neither rising nor falling — the only tone that feels "normal" to English ears
starts low and falls slowly, like a tired sigh
dips a little then rises again, like a doubtful "huh?" — one curved movement
rises like *sắc* but **catches in the middle**, a small break in the throat
drops short and stops abruptly, the throat closes — the syllable becomes the shortest

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note that the tone mark always sits **above or below a vowel**, and it is different from the marks that change **the vowel's sound** (*ă*, *â*, *ê*, *ô*, *ơ*, *ư*). One letter can carry both at once: *ệ* = the letter *ê* with the *nặng* tone; *ướ* = *ư* and *ơ* with the *sắc* tone. Don't panic at the pile-up — read it in two steps: first which letter, then which tone.

blocks.title: The three tone pairs learners mix up most
items: ***hỏi* vs *ngã*** — both rise, and even native speakers in the south merge them. At A1 you **may** read *ngã* like *hỏi*; you will still be understood. What you may not do is read both flat.
***huyền* vs *nặng*** — both are low, but *huyền* is **long and gliding down**, while *nặng* is **short and stops dead**. Practice with the pair *và* (and) versus *vạ* — long versus clipped.

***sắc* vs *ngang*** — they look easiest to tell apart, yet they get swapped most, because English raises the voice at the end of questions and lists. *Cà phê* (coffee) often comes out as *cá phê*, and *cá* means fish.

blocks.text: Consonants that don't sound the way you'd guess
This is the most important list after the tones, and it is only fourteen lines long. The **Say it** column throughout the course applies this list for you, so you never have to work it out yourself.

head: Written
Our spelling
How it sounds
Example
rows: *s* as in "sun"; in the north the two are the same
*ch* as in "chin", but softer; in the north the two are the same
*t* with a strong puff of air, as in "top" — **never** as in "think"
a breathy *k*, like *ch* in Scottish "loch" or German "Bach"
*k* as in "skin" — no puff of air
*ng* as in "singer" — also at the **start** of a word
read as written (*t* without a puff, as in "stop")

blocks.text: ⚠️ Two lines deserve repeating because they are tripped over most: **d is not *d***, but *z*. The letter that sounds like *d* is **đ** (with a bar through it). The city of *Đà Nẵng* is said with a *d*, but *dạ* (yes) is said "zạ". One small bar, a completely different sound. And **th is never the *th* of "think"** — it is just a breathy *t*.
Final consonants: held, not released

English often releases a final consonant with a little burst of air: "cat" ends with an audible *t*. Vietnamese **holds it**: the mouth takes the position and stops there, with no air coming out — like the *t* in a quick "that one", or the *p* in "yup!".

blocks.text: The vowels — keep the letters, learn their sounds

Vietnamese has eleven vowel sounds, and several have no English equivalent. In the **Say it** column **we keep the original vowel letters** with all their marks — precisely so your eyes get used to recognizing them, rather than hiding them behind English spellings that would be wrong anyway.

head: Letter
How it sounds
How to practice
Example
rows: a long "uh", like *u* in "fur" without the *r*
say "uh" and hold it twice as long
same as *ơ* but cut off quickly
between *i* and *u*: tongue as for "oo", but lips spread, **not** rounded
say "oo", then pull your lips into a smile without changing the sound
a **short**, clipped *a*, as in "cut" said fast
"ay" as in "say", but pure — no glide into *ee*
*ô* = a pure "oh" (no glide into *w*); *o* = an open "aw" as in "law"
*tô* (bowl) versus *to* (big) — rounded lips for *ô*, open mouth for *o*

blocks.text: The rest: *a* = "ah" as in "father", *i* and *y* = "ee" as in "see", *u* = "oo" as in "food", *e* = "eh" as in "bed" (more open). Vowel clusters are read in sequence without a break: *ai* → "ah-ee" (like "eye"), *ao* → "ah-o" (like "ow"), *êu* → *ê* + "oo", *ươ* → *ư* + *ơ*.

blocks.title: How to read the "Say it" column in this course
items: The Say it column **respells the consonants** (*x*→s, *ch*/*tr*→ch, *nh*→ny, *đ*→d, *d*→z …) and **keeps the vowel letters and all tone marks** exactly as written.

So *xin chào* appears as **sin chào**, *cảm ơn* as **kảm ơn**, *phòng trọ* as **fòng chọ**. Only what would mislead your eyes changes; the tones and the special vowels stay visible, because those are exactly what you have to learn.
If a word has no letter that needs changing, the column will look the same as the original. That's not a misprint — it means the word is read as written.

blocks.text: No stress — and that's a big gift

Vietnamese has **no word stress** at all. Every syllable gets the same weight — because the weight is already being used to carry the tone. That is a huge saving compared with English, Russian or Italian, where stress has to be learned word by word.

In exchange: almost every Vietnamese word is **one syllable**, and longer words are really several one-syllable words written separately. *Việt Nam* is two words. *Bệnh viện* (hospital) is two words: *bệnh* (illness) + *viện* (institute) — an "illness institute". Once you notice this, Vietnamese vocabulary stops feeling like blind memorization and starts feeling like building with blocks.
What Vietnamese does NOT have
This list comes first on purpose, because half the effort of learning a foreign language usually goes into the things below — and here not one of them needs to be learned.

head: Not there
What it means for you
Example
rows: *đi* stays *đi* for anyone, at any time
one form for one and for many
time is marked by separate words *đã / đang / sẽ*
every syllable has the same weight

blocks.text: ⚠️ The same word is used for **"I" and "you"** depending on who is speaking. A young woman calls the person she is talking to *anh* and calls herself *em*; he calls himself *anh* and calls her *em*. What decides is not the person, but **the age gap**.
Time markers
Asking questions
⚠️ **Question words stay in place**; they are not moved to the front as in English. *Anh đi đâu?* is literally "you go where?", not "where do you go?".
Classifiers used at A1
Numbers

⚠️ Three exceptions to memorize: **5** becomes *lăm* after tens (*mười lăm*, *hai mươi lăm*); **1** becomes *mốt* after tens other than *mười* (*hai mươi mốt*); **10** becomes *mươi* inside multiples of ten (*hai mươi*, not *hai mười*).
Helper verbs & chained verbs
Verbs **line up directly** with nothing in between: *tôi muốn đi ăn cơm* = "I want go eat rice" — no "to", no "-ing". This is one of the most relieving things in the whole language.
Little words at the end of the sentence

head: Word
Function
English feel
Example
rows: shows respect; required with older people
a soft invitation, asks for agreement
seeks agreement on a shared impression
turns a statement into a question

blocks.text: This group of words is what turns your Vietnamese from "correct" into "sounding like a person". English does the same job with tone of voice and tag questions ("isn't it?", "you know", "come on"); Vietnamese packs it into one small word. Unit 17 covers them in full.

If you have reached this page after working through all twenty units, you now have roughly 700 words and the whole basic structure of A1 Vietnamese: you can greet people with the right pronoun, ask and deny, shop and bargain, order food, tell the time, talk about the past, compare, handle errands at the post office and the hospital, and soften your sentences with little words at the end.

The one thing you don't have yet cannot be given by a printed page: **an ear**. Tones don't come in through the eyes. From now on, the rest of your progress depends on how much Vietnamese you hear, not how much you read.

blocks.title: Three steps after this course
items: **Listen every day, twenty minutes, without reading the text.** Beginner podcasts, slow news, songs — anything, as long as it is northern Vietnamese. You don't need to understand; you are training your ear to tell six tones apart, and that is work for the ear, not the head.

**Talk to people, and let yourself get tones wrong.** Tone mistakes are almost always funny, almost never offensive. Vietnamese people are famously warm toward foreigners who try their language, and very few foreigners try — you will be welcomed far more warmly than you imagine.

**Move up to A2 by adding words, not rules.** This is how Vietnamese differs from European languages: no next mountain of grammar is waiting. A2 and B1 are almost entirely about vocabulary and flexibility, not new forms to memorize. The grammar you hold now is nearly all the grammar there is.

blocks.text: *Chúc bạn nhiều may mắn — và hẹn gặp lại!*
